query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Inserting a nanometer‐scale Nb interlayer between adjacent HEA layers will promote a controlled, gradual transition from diffusion‐mediated creep at higher temperatures to dislocation‐mediated creep under lower temperature or higher stress conditions by tuning the interface coherency.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers with coherent or semi‐coherent interfaces
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin elemental niobium (Nb) interlayer between the HEA layers
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep conditions typical for advanced coating applications; tests under varying temperatures and applied stresses
generation.structural_mediator: The coherency maintained at the HEA/Nb interfaces
generation.mechanism: Nb’s moderate diffusivity and close lattice match with many HEAs allow it to form coherent interfaces. At elevated temperatures, the Nb layer facilitates enhanced atomic diffusion at the interface, favoring diffusion-controlled creep. Under lower temperatures or higher applied stresses, the same interface can support the nucleation and movement of dislocations, favoring dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with multilayers lacking the Nb interlayer, the modified system will exhibit a smoother and more predictable transition in creep mechanisms, observable as a shift in creep strain rate and deformation mode when moving from high to moderate temperature/stress conditions.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without a distinct Nb transitional layer, where the transition between creep mechanisms is less controlled and may lead to nonuniform interfacial deformation.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if the Nb layer remains thin enough to maintain coherent or semi‐coherent interfaces; if the layer becomes too thick, it might result in interfacial discontinuities or phase mismatches that could negate the intended mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and temperature/stress windows for the Nb layer’s effectiveness are not fully determined and require further joint experimental and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer coatings—one with a thin (e.g., several nanometers) Nb interlayer and one without. Conduct high-temperature creep tests over a range of temperatures and applied stresses. Use in situ TEM and XRD to monitor the evolution of interfacial coherency and the dominant creep mechanisms.
measurements: Creep strain rates as a function of temperature and stress
Interface coherency metrics via high-resolution imaging
Activation energy derived from creep curves
Dislocation density and diffusion path signatures at the interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the insertion of the Nb interlayer does not yield a significant change in the creep behavior—specifically, if no measurable shift in the transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep is observed and the interface coherency does not improve compared to the baseline HEA multilayers—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

frame.system: High‐entropy alloy (HEA) multilayer coatings – these are composite materials composed of HEA layers designed for excellent mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance, with interfaces whose coherency is critical.
frame.goal: To identify and justify a material for the interface (or interlayer) that can mediate a transition between diffusion‐mediated creep and dislocation‐mediated creep, clarifying the role of interface coherency in creep behavior.
frame.limitation: The exact mechanism by which interface coherency influences the creep mechanism in HEA multilayers is not fully understood, leaving the proper choice of a transitional material ambiguous.
root_cause_cues: specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior remains unclear
transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
constraints: the selected material must be compatible with HEA layers (i.e. form coherent or semi‐coherent interfaces),
it must enable a smooth transition between diffusion-controlled processes (such as grain-boundary or interface diffusion) and dislocation-based creep,
it should not compromise the overall corrosion resistance, irradiation tolerance, or mechanical properties of the multilayer system
frame.regime: High-temperature creep conditions where both diffusion creep and dislocation creep mechanisms may be active; the operating regime typically involves stress and temperature levels where interface behavior critically affects creep rates.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have highlighted the excellent properties of HEA multilayers but left the impact of interface coherency on the creep transition largely unexplained.

Earlier designs often assumed that a coherent interface is universally beneficial; however, the lack of clarity in the transition between diffusion- and dislocation-mediated mechanisms has limited targeted material selection for the transitional layer.

families.principle: Integrate experimental measurements with computational simulations to iteratively refine understanding of interfacial phenomena, bridging the gap between empirical observations and theoretical predictions in the creep transition.
cues_for: role of interface coherency is unclear and has been difficult to isolate using either approach alone
constraints demand compatibility with HEA layers while enabling smooth mechanistic transition
cues_against: previous attempts have not fully resolved the mechanistic role of the interface, suggesting that a single approach may not be sufficient
families.best_lever: Couple in situ characterization techniques with atomistic simulations to directly link observed interfacial structure changes (e.g., coherency levels) with predicted mechanical response, thereby identifying the optimal transitional material.

families.principle: Directly observe the evolution of the interfacial microstructure and defect activity in real time under high-temperature creep conditions, linking changes in coherency with transitions in deformation mechanisms.
cues_for: specific role of interface coherency on creep behavior
transition between diffusion-controlled and dislocation-controlled mechanisms
cues_against: the limited clarity in the impact of interface coherency on the mechanism suggests that even high-resolution imaging might miss transient or nanoscale phenomena
previous studies did not fully explain this mechanism through characterization alone
families.best_lever: Employ in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) or synchrotron-based techniques during creep tests to capture real-time changes at the interfaces.

families.principle: Use computational models to simulate atomistic diffusion and dislocation interactions at coherent and semi-coherent interfaces, thereby predicting how different interlayer materials influence the creep mechanism transition.
cues_for: unclear mechanism in transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep
need to understand how specific interfacial properties affect defect mobility
cues_against: simulations alone might not capture all the environmental and operational complexities (e.g., irradiation, corrosion) unless validated against experiments
families.best_lever: Develop atomistic or mesoscale models that incorporate realistic interfacial structures and simulate creep behavior under high-temperature and stress conditions, guiding which interlayer material offers optimal transition characteristics.

families.principle: Isolate and systematically vary the interfacial material properties (e.g., composition, thickness) to observe changes in creep behavior, thereby directly probing how variations in interface coherency mediate the transition between diffusion‐mediated and dislocation‐mediated mechanisms.
cues_for: transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
cues_against: the exact mechanism remains unclear, indicating that simple variable tests may not capture all underlying atomic-scale phenomena

families.best_lever: Adjust and control the interlayer composition or thickness to create coherent or semi‐coherent interfaces, then measure creep rates under high-temperature conditions to identify any threshold behavior.
